items.text: “We’re at 712 month” — tracking a little behind where we were at the same time last year, but with a pretty reasonable amount of quotes outstanding as well. Plenty of goals to chase and a whole lot of month still ahead of us, so a reasonable position so far.
Ahead of last year on soil tests, just a little behind on sap, and total tests very comparable at 1,044 v 1,072. We’re about to start getting busy in that space.
Waiting on their side, with a contact change there — expecting to hear today or early next week.
Just the freight cost to add for the blend, then updating and confirming it today.
The $0 quote — should be easy to push through; numbers being worked up now.

Open orders summarised across the three columns — not yet shipped, in fulfilment or in transit, partially delivered — with the original delivery date, the updated schedule date and any notes on each card, plus stock on hand showing committed, incoming and forecast.
The data was pulled Thursday, so a couple of orders had already gone out by the meeting. The plan is to pull first thing on meeting morning so everything is current.

The day counts run off the original delivery date entered in Odoo, which makes some orders look further out than they really are — one had been re-scheduled because Hamilton was tweaking the mix. That’s one of the nips and tucks to come.
Entered into the dashboard for now; the plan is to pull them live out of the Odoo log notes so it’s one condensed view.
Jamie shares this link after every sales meeting — scroll to your own customers, and click through to any order in Odoo to add detail yourself.

An excellent event from an industry standpoint and well worth attending next time, ideally with more weeks to prepare. The learning: people come to look at seed plots and listen to talks — it only runs every three years — and the way the trial sites were situated, a chemical or fertiliser trial got very little traffic compared with the exhibitor stands.

Excess nitrogen in the standard (middle, conventional) program. The right-hand side was a screw-up — somewhere between 500 and 800 kg of rustica went on over the top, potentially an extra 90 units of N, and the plants were soft. The interesting result: the Hybrid Ag liquid program over a low rate of Pearl Fusion, effectively equivalent to their 12.5.14 in the middle, still produced pretty decent results. Difference showed in root mass, side hairs, and how the leaf held up with no refrigeration or post-harvest management.

Nathan and Jamie’s shared Google sheet takes every lead from every campaign and source, and feeds this dashboard so the whole team can see what’s hot and what’s being nurtured. Nathan calls certain leads to cover ground alongside Jamie; when one’s good to go Jamie contacts the agronomist and it slots into the CRM.
Nathan is working through the exact rollout plan with Jamie and confirming the best burst play. Horticulture, not broadacre — three assets: a video from Smithy plus two statics.
Past campaigns are moving into their own pill so the tab focuses on what’s ahead. Fruit Growers Victoria is being pulled together now.

Horticulture-specific, chasing new business in the small veg space alongside Hamilton, and taking some pressure off Chelsea’s region. A sharp operator last time round, back with four years of new skills.
Jamie is working on this financial year’s forecast and will start with a phone call to everyone individually, looking to book 30–60 minutes each over the next fortnight.
Jamie is making contact to coincide with the new SP launch; the aim is Friday 31 July, in lieu of the technical meeting, to walk through the new products and brand. Not locked in yet.

Started this week and back five days a week from Monday. She’s the main point of contact for chasing orders and deliveries, contactable on the landline, and already set up on WhatsApp — number to be circulated. She’ll reach out proactively ahead of orders going out and production being executed, so the team gets visibility in advance.

Held in German customs and now about three weeks late for Jimmy Kellaher, Dan McGrath and Ron Kazitzki (Selby Pastoral). The samples are well spoiled, so they’ll need retesting — another reason Jimmy is leaning further towards AgVita. Paige has been chasing and getting stuffed around too; DHL shows a customs release but it still hasn’t landed. Jamie is investigating and will email the team if there’s anything useful in it.
Raised on the call: NovaCropControl normally comes back around the two-week mark. Past three weeks, is there any point listening to the data — or paying for the test?

Shout-out of the week. He reached out unprompted about how he runs the CRM, wanting to get on the front foot before the one-on-ones — “good to see a gentleman like Woody happy to put his hand up when there’s something he doesn’t know.”
Got a genuine workout later in the meeting — new team members hearing it for the first time, and it framed the accommodation-booking discussion: if there’s a better system, we’ll look at it.
$890k confirmed for July with another week to run, and about $160k of quotes sitting in the system. Lagging a little behind the same time last year — with a fair idea of where that’s come from.
Chelsea flying along at the top for the month, Jimmy not far behind.
Soil tests neck-and-neck with last year and flying along for the month; leaf tests down a little — watching for them to tick up.
Section still being straightened out — disregard for now.

Hamilton’s spuds order still sitting as-is — followed Steve up Wednesday, waiting on him to pull the trigger. Woody’s quote restructured this morning: the client doesn’t want the whole order at once, so it’s staged now.

All boards carry notes now — jump in and read anything relevant before chasing someone. Amos announced this page as a live document pulling from Odoo hourly (“thanks to a bit of handiwork behind the scenes from Katseli”) — the link goes out to the team after the meeting.
About two days behind schedule; next week looks reasonably free, so back on top early in the week.

Two semi loads picked up this morning, the final load out this afternoon or Monday, and the spreader on its way for delivery tomorrow. The transport company dragged its feet — that freight sat ready for a week.

Amos and Nate meet Janelle Monday morning: how ops information flows to the team, how she communicates freight delays back to clients, and pulling her Odoo notes into this dashboard so it becomes the central hub. More to the team next Friday.

Weekly Activity now shows every story from the week with posts pulling through too; the Stats pill is evolving; and the marketing calendar is live — brand book, event retros, the frost post that went out late last night, and the bud-development post in the works.

Clear breakdown of every lead tracked so far, where they came from and where they’re at. Nurturing toward appointments; a testing offer is going to the Playbook “no” cohort to pull them into interested.

Some names on the list are already close to Hybrid (Dan Hill for one) — a cold-ish follow-up could read disconnected. Nathan to call Nate and walk through exactly what’s been sent; cross-checking against existing customers is already underway, and the one-on-ones give TMs visibility.
9:00 Eastern next week — Amos to send the calendar invite.
In place of the technical huddle: Grant and Kamal from Great Southern Biology on the two new products, plus a rehash on Lockout — bring questions beforehand so we’re armed and dangerous.

Reminder from Roselle via Jamie: a few days’ notice where possible gives her more options on rooms. Jimmy proposed a booking app with an approval flow instead of screenshot-and-email double handling — “no sacred cows”; Jamie’s looking at it and will grab details on the Cherry Hill call.

Request for an updated org chart / points of contact for vehicles, accommodation and the like — possibly next Friday with Amos. Noted: a point-of-contact doc already lives in the Odoo knowledge section; keep that the single location.
Smithy is up for Mojo on Monday.

Jamie called out the Montague work in front of the team — “absolutely phenomenal” — for the effort put into that relationship and where it has got us. Ticks optimising inputs, maximising outcomes and transforming food for health, with integrity, finding a way and knowledge all through it. The Koori Fruit presentation the same week got its own mention: sniffing out opportunities and bringing them back to the business, even where they sit a little left of field of what we normally do.
Very broadacre-dominant — not much hort action in the group chat. Full attribution sits under each photo above.

Jimmy’s leaf shot is the worst brailing he has seen. Around 100–150 mL/ha of a 25% molybdenum liquid had gone on, not ours, plus a fair bit of fungal disease. Nate’s aside: treat crops more like zucchinis and feed them up on moly.

Bruce’s Warda beans on Graeme Stevenson’s river flats — a problem paddock for years, high silica and dries out fast regardless of irrigation. 120 kg/ha seed, kieserite as starter on the grower’s call. Sap tested Wednesday; boron and molybdenum expected, but test rather than guess.

The Boyd pasture at Young is swamped — nettles a metre high across a third of the paddock. Both indicate biological activity with poor digestion of organic matter, and it isn’t a stock camp. Turned into the tangent of the morning: marshmallow was originally a food crop, and nettle picked before flowering is good for inflammation if you blanch the sting out. Woody has volunteered to try it.
Sitting at $1.5M on the last day of the month. Add the $203k of open quotes and we are on par with where we were last year. A strong final week clawed back a lot of the gap.

Chelsea’s Montague quote looks imminent once the PO is over the line. Hamilton has spoken to Steve again on Hamp and will try going direct next week if nothing more comes back. Nothing else in the list Jamie wasn’t already across.
Flying at the moment — a big contribution this month, and it ties straight back into the Montague relationship work.

Soil tests knocked out of the park this month; leaf looked well down. Jimmy’s read for broadacre: growers have been jumping on nitrogen and the usual traces off last season’s data, so the work has come through as an order rather than a fresh sap test. Jamie: year to date we are not far off the pace, and the broadacre season is running earlier this year, so some of these tests landed a month ago or will land next month.

Nathan asked whether the AgVita tests were included in the figures; Chelsea to double-check the number. Bruce confirmed he has been doing a lot more through AgVita this season especially. Nathan to set up a split so it is clear how many DSAs versus SAPs — the Sales tab now breaks leaf testing out by lab.

Amos walked the screen. Smiths ready, waiting on the last few bags to be picked up. Jason Allen had a Humix on back order, going out today. Lenco waiting on them to collect the remaining IBCs. Nightingale’s digestate has landed and just needs to get up to them, plus a small blend for Alex Grant. The Young-area orders are ready and waiting on transport to confirm pickup.

Bragars delivered yesterday, Vivo and the Dunes went out yesterday, GB Crop amended their order, Yamatry goes this afternoon with another to follow Monday or Tuesday. Several of these still read as behind because the updates haven’t been pushed through in Odoo yet.

Yamatry was held by a calcium nitrate delivery pushed back a couple of days. A couple of small orders are waiting on lab tests for the organic side. Torrance is being delivered direct by Peats Soils, about three quarters done with the rest next week. Mity Jones asked to push back on wet paddocks. CC has moved to August. Red Rock is waiting on the remainder of the gypsum, being mixed as we spoke.

Still waiting on payment. Luke said he would have organised it on 23 July and is back from Ireland; nothing had come through as of early this week. Nathan asked whether we had checked it had cleared recently — Amos to follow up.

Internal story-share goals held. The Fruit Growers Victoria content has started rolling out and the whole campaign is now in the dashboard — every day of the conference, with content built out to today and the next five days in progress. Works well on mobile. The Bud Optimisation post went out this morning.

A few good organic enquiries in, notes attached, Jamie working them. On the Cherry Playbook campaign, a heap of people only wanted the booklet, so they got a follow-up email and text earlier this week with a testing offer. Not the strongest play, deliberately a test of the water — if it doesn’t convert, the next batch gets a slightly better offer.

Bruce asked whether posts with a person in them — like Jimmy’s paddock piece — engage better than those without, and whether we have the numbers to prove it. The stats tab is basic today; view rates and deeper analytics can be pulled and that is on the list. Jimmy wants to keep putting himself and others on camera as a different level of engagement.

Following Bruce’s request last week, the Contacts button in the top corner of this dashboard now gives a directory of who to direct what to. Janelle isn’t in it yet — some of Amos’s items shift across as her role firms up — and more detail on vehicles and the like can go in over time.

A Pricelist tab has been added in the same corner as an easy reference, with organic status against each product. Disregard the organic information for now — Amos is still waiting on ACO. Once it lands you will be able to segment by what is ACO-approved, and anything restricted will explain its restrictions on hover. Should be complete within a couple of weeks.

On hold roughly 6–8 weeks. The acetic acid in the calcium acetate needs a paper trail proving a non-synthetic source, which we can’t currently provide, so new stock has been reordered. Nate and Chelsea are most affected. We are playing it by the book rather than in the grey. In the interim there are a couple of organic calcium products we can give a general recommendation on — and they run $50–$80 dearer per 20 L than ours, which softens the conversation.

Nathan asked how labelling works. Dry and prescription blends are part of the labelling process, but the certification is applied for at the time of producing each blend rather than once for the range. You would expect approval of every raw ingredient to carry through to the finished blend; it doesn’t. Bruce asked whether that means testing the blend after manufacture — no: liquids need heavy-metal testing before release, dry blends don’t, and the certification rests on the raw ingredients. Frustrating, but clear.
Out of action for surgery early next week. Anything that falls on Monday or Tuesday, call today.

Jimmy’s standing question, brought to the group: the two labs give genuinely different results and a different recommendation off the same paddock. He screen-shared both reports side by side — wheat at Morris, near Rand, same leaf taken (AgVita’s youngest mature leaf against NovaCrop’s young leaf).

AgVita: no detectable nitrate and high molybdenum. NovaCrop: reasonable nitrate, lower moly. Copper reads satisfactory on AgVita but low on both leaves on NovaCrop, and a third the value in the young leaf. Boron similar — Jimmy doesn’t accept AgVita’s optimal range there. Zinc slightly higher on NovaCrop. Brix 6–7 on the refractometer against 11.7 on the AgVita report, and sugar reads low on NovaCrop.

Potassium is close — 7,000 against 6,100. Iron is low on both. Hamilton’s read: a similar fingerprint overall, with nitrogen moved around. Jamie has seen this before at Cherry Hill two seasons ago: majors line up, traces don’t, because traces are far harder to extract consistently and it comes down to lab methodology, not one lab being right.

Jamie’s approach, offered up deliberately to be challenged: ignore the ammonium and nitrate split and go to total nitrogen — the actual energy outcome in the plant. Young leaf sitting well ahead of old leaf signals an oncoming deficiency regardless of what the other forms are doing, and there aren’t large reserves in the others on a parts basis. The same differential argues an oncoming phosphorus deficiency too, with phosphorus applied as straight MAP at 80 kg/ha.

Copper and boron definitely. Some molybdenum only if applying nitrate forms — and he won’t be, because he doesn’t want to push more tillers into what looks like a dry spring. Walking the paddock, it looks nitrogen hungry, which is what the AgVita test says and the NovaCrop test doesn’t.

There has been no molybdenum applied on that paddock beyond a sodium molybdate in a legume rotation a while back. On that basis Jamie would bin AgVita’s moly result outright. Hort is not using AgVita much, though it gets used early season where a grower wants results fast, with a NovaCrop test to back it up.
The best fertiliser recommendations still come from walking the paddock yourself and getting a feel for it. Use the test as side rails, not as the answer.

Put health itself under the Transforming Food for Health banner — a reminder that we all contribute, on a pretty widespread scale, to the health of the general population or to the poor health of it. The work question that falls out of it: are we really doing everything we can to produce the best food, and the healthiest people, that we can?

Ask someone how they are and genuinely listen to the answer before launching into the reason for the call — they may not have the energy for what you came to talk about, and you would never know. Jamie’s addition: are you asking for a response, or is it just the thing we all say in passing while tuning out the answer?
Nate’s pistachios, Jimmy’s wheat, Bruce’s nutrient-removal table and Woody’s macadamias. Full detail sits under each photo above.

The pistachio block turned into the morning’s tangent: lasered wall-to-wall plantings as biological deserts, and whether anything can live in the strips between rows. Woody’s Bundaberg example runs 8 km of fence line, macadamia the whole way, no shelter belts. Nobody could name a tree crop planted as a genuine multi-species system at scale — mid-row cover crops are as far as it goes, and without reliable rainfall the seed cost is hard to justify.

Off the back of Jimmy’s canola: a grower at Rand is lining up a third sclerotinia spray on the agronomist’s word rather than on anything he has seen. Bruce’s counter — five passes at Roger Robinson’s a couple of seasons ago still came back below par. If you are going to use a fungicide, make sure it actually works: water quality or tank pH can strip 30–40% of its capacity, which is a fine outcome for soil health and no outcome at all for the disease. That ran into chlorinated town water in the tank, and a question to put back to Great Southern Biology about what it does to a biological mix.

$364k month to date with another $140k in open quotes. Last August was a very good month, so the number being chased is a big one and we are lagging month on month — but a lot is starting to make its way through, and Jamie expects it to even out as the month goes on.
Still absolutely flying for the financial year.
Still to come back to.

Amos walked the outstanding orders, with the caveat that a couple read as behind only because Odoo hasn’t caught up — the notes are accurate, the records lag. Montague’s blends and Pearl Fusion delivered with liquids scheduled early next week; Finley Park taking one load today and one tomorrow, with the spreader riding on one of them via the rigid truck on hire; Smiths Fruit picked up; Bale citrus blooms done; ColourMax in production for dispatch today or Monday; the Darren Hayes strawberry blend product landed yesterday and goes today; Ingelara partially delivered; Red Rock down to the liquid gypsum back-order.

Soluble calcium yet to arrive on one order. A couple of organic lines sit on final test results and label approval. Torrens Valley is being delivered direct by Peats Soils — waiting on their update. Came through as a lead; Amos and Nathan went through it yesterday and it has converted — five tonnes of Cal ordered. Jamie had left a message with him that morning without hearing back.

items.lead: What the stats can tell us
items.text: Answering Nate’s question: stories genuinely only carry views, reach and taps. Posts carry far more, and it is all on the dashboard now. We are also experimenting with very small boosts — the frost / BudMax post shows the view count climbing sharply for not much spend.

The Fruit Growers Victoria campaign is running, with another boosted post to come as a key part of it. Great Southern Biology product updates are still being worked in the background. On leads, a few good enquiries last week with Jamie working them — Leon is the most recent.

Now in the Pricing tab. A lot of background work with Trina and Amos: the stock variations didn’t have correct Odoo entries, and now every one does — cost price set, linked directly through. The question came up about the blocked citrus samples. Josh’s Burquettes submission was held for a separate customs check and never went further; Jimmy’s went through. The fix is putting the species name on the form, where the habit had been to leave the crop/variety field blank — never a problem until this one. Woody’s recollection for citrus was a reticulata-type name, but he wasn’t certain, so worth pinning down properly before the next submission.

mtg-notes-0807.title: AI, and what cuts through it

items.text: Shared a marketing email from a company whose material he normally finds genuinely useful, and this one told him nothing he wanted to know about the product. The tells: repeated words nobody actually says, and sentences that lecture rather than lead — someone else added the dashes, “every time I see dashes, I know it’s AI.” First time their email read like something he could have got out of ChatGPT himself.

What cuts through the noise is a customer reading an email and knowing Hamilton wrote it. AI is a powerful tool and it is not going away, but there is a widening window for things that feel human — at a marketing and a sales level — and everyone leaning on the machine falls by the wayside in it. Where you have the time, form your own thoughts and write your own emails.

The Maxsil segment on Landline a fortnight ago has generated at least five unprompted grower conversations for one of the team, and “heaps” for another. Nothing sciency about it — footage of sampling and running the tools — and growers who knew nothing about silica now feel like they do, and want some.

Woody flagged a video on the AEA site: a handheld nutrient monitor reading leaf and producing a mix on the spot, results immediately. Jamie has chased the supplier three times through their support line, off the back of a Canoponics conversation about testing issues — they have a customer who wants to buy one and run trials — and has had nothing back. Presumably inundated.

mtg-notes-0814.title: Values — speed from conversation to outcome

items.text: Handed the values shout-out to Nathan against Find a Way and Learn, Challenge, Improve; Repeat — the speed at which something goes from a casual conversation to a finished thing. The example was that morning: a passing suggestion about a fix he assumed would take a fortnight, already done by the time he sat down.
Bruce’s triticale and his composted manure pile, Nate Strawbridge’s Commodus barley and Chelsea’s Montague stone fruit. Full detail sits under each photo above.

Both of Bruce’s shots came with questions and he wasn’t on the call. The triticale is the live one — over east it is planted deliberately, where in WA it mostly turns up out of dirty wheat seed, and what it is being grown for is worth asking. The composted manure at Australian Fresh Milk Holdings is the other.

Lagging last year by a fair margin, and Jamie’s read is that the shape of the month matters as much as the number: at the same day last year we were at $1.7M and only finished at $2.5M, so most of last August landed early. The gap now is not the gap at month end.

Jamie is finishing a workbook comparing the top 20 clients for August last year against August so far this year. The drop-off is immense and the list is a very different one. Some of it is timing rather than loss — Hamilton’s example was Wormtech, big orders last August and expected end of September this year. It goes out to the team to cast eyes over; if a client on it looks explainable, say so.

Last year is no longer the right benchmark, because the business has gone backwards against it. What the graph needs is the month’s budget carried across the days, so the question becomes where we should be today rather than where we were a year ago. Hamilton’s working figure was around $2.45M for the month and roughly $1,170k by the 13th.

Contribution Margin by Territory Manager comes off — the data isn’t pulling through correctly, so it goes rather than sits there wrong. FYTD Total Sales by Territory Manager takes its place, with a month-to-date version beside it so the year and the month read side by side.
Still tracking about on par with last year once the AgVita SAP tests are counted in.

Amos walked the overdue orders. Rich Glenn in production and close to finished; Smok and one other for dispatch that day; Bale sent Thursday; Knight dispatched Thursday; Nutrien picked up that day. CRC is a placeholder against the Hussey order and waiting on the customer to confirm a delivery date. One load is sitting finished and ready, waiting on Gus Campbell to collect. The Montague orders are either delivered, going that day, or Monday.
Booked for dispatch Monday. The original blend wasn’t working as a liquid, so it was tweaked and re-sampled to be sure before it goes.

Hamilton needs Rich Glenn on the ground for an application early next week — Amos is aiming for Friday afternoon or Monday. For Ellie, Chris is happy to take delivery and hold it in the shed so it is ready the moment they hear back, rather than wait. Amos is calling him Monday on the calcium; it may be a swap, or the liquids go and the rest follows once Zadco lands.

Additional charges on a separate invoice line generate the most questions of anything we send out. The cost behind it is real: a part shuttle takes the same pallet space and the same truck, we still buy the IBC, and on return we pay to ship it back, clean it, inspect it and sometimes cut it up. That is margin, and growers should hear about it at quote time rather than discover it on an invoice.

Build the charge into the per-litre price when quoting and explain it there. Jamie’s framing for the conversation: price 200 L in 20s against 200 L in a part shuttle, and be straight that most competitors won’t do part shuttles at all — even with the fee the grower is better off.

Not settled, deliberately, with the room thin. Chelsea prefers it built in and asked for it in writing to mull over. Hamilton pointed out the separate line exists for certified partners, whose own calculations have to reconcile with ours. Nathan adds the fee himself on CP quotes and was blunt that the old build-in-then-divide-back approach was painful with codes in Xero, where a flat part-shuttle charge has been a breeze. The likely landing is a line item for CPs and built into the price direct to customer. Jamie is sending the detail round by email and it gets hashed out with more of the team present.
Which mechanism we pick is close to negligible. What matters is that the conversation happens up front, so nobody is surprised.

items.lead: Heavy metals — wider than we thought
items.text: The agreement covers the whole range for heavy metal testing, not just the one product that raised the issue. That was understood as product-specific along the chain and wasn’t — Jamie and Amos both put their hand up for it. Away now: Aminoplex (result already back, sent July), FKF, K-Max, OptiCal and PowerCal, and OptiTrace boron, copper, iron, manganese, moly and zinc. Amos is reconciling the rest against the full organic list and sending the gaps. Turnaround is 7–10 business days. If an order is held awaiting a heavy metals test, that is why.

Testing is per batch, so a new batch needs a new test. Nate should forecast organic traces into the system even where orders aren’t firm, so stock-take shows a batch running low early enough to get testing underway. BudMax and OptiTrace Max are going forward now for the organic growers coming into spring. It is an ongoing requirement, though a run of clean results makes it a fair conversation at the next audit.

All approved except FKF, K-Max and 0030 — positioning of information and some additional asterisks. Amos has resubmitted and the request is confirmed as processed, with approval expected shortly. Product can technically ship without the label, since it is the label and not the product that is outstanding.

Effectively Chelsea and Nate. Bruce has an organic wheat grower who uses very little and Jimmy an organic garlic grower doing small volumes; nothing significant in Queensland. Jamie’s call is to over-communicate it anyway so the whole team can answer the question if it comes up. Worth noting the direction of travel: 2026 is the biggest organic batch we have ever made, in 30,000 L runs.

Montague hold about 18 shuttles of calcium chloride bought through a tender, and want it gone rather than carried into next year. They don’t have to use all of it. Their preference was the apples, to maximise calcium; cherries were raised and steered away from. They are not replacing PowerCal — this is on top.

Chelsea inferred it was in the system before anyone told her: leaf chloride was significantly high last year with no matching soil chloride. She asked point blank whether they were spraying calcium chloride and was told no — which was probably honest, because the label reads Cal 175 and, as Hamilton put it, growers often have no idea what form they are using. That sent everyone down a rabbit hole of water quality and Humix at the rhizosphere. Colour in their Pinks is their biggest hindrance, and excess chloride does much the same thing as nitrogen applied too late.

Cal 175 is 17.5% calcium and 31% chloride. Ten foliar applications at 10 L/ha puts about 31 units of chloride straight onto the leaf, against a soil test that might total something similar. For a highly mobile nutrient Hamilton called that a no-go zone.

Fertigate it, don’t spray it — in with the OptiCal fertigation at late flower, the same trick already used to carry leftover thiocal and thio-K in on an existing application rather than adding a pass. 50 L/ha, potentially up to 100. Fertigated, the chloride displaces through the soil instead of sitting on leaf and fruit; it disassociates almost immediately and about 75 mm of rain moves the lot, which is why soil tests before and after rain read so differently. The young trees are the better home for it than the mature blocks — 18 ha, already on a fortnightly fertigation, growth lost last year to make up, and chloride is a vegetative nutrient. The seven hectares of pears won’t make a dent. Leaf tests through the season, and cut it the moment chloride climbs.

If the product weren’t already sitting on the farm with a requirement to use it up, nobody here would put it in the program. It isn’t that it is bad — it is a lot of calcium, cheap, and reasonably cost-effective fertigated — it is that the program doesn’t need it. Tuesday’s session with Montague partly exists so their team knows where not to use it; some have already gone rogue with PowerCal and OptiTrace boron, which are better things to go rogue with.

Working through the list — FKF, BudMax and the Great Southern Biology products. OptiCal and PowerCal are on the desk now, and the forms discussion above goes straight into them: five concepts for the last page, with a comparison of forms the likely pick as a tasteful way in rather than going straight at a product. Hamilton’s addition — make sure salt index is in there. Chelsea is sending her forms table through.
A brief has gone to Grant as a dashboard — every brochure draft plus the questions still outstanding, so his answers come back before anything goes out.

Thursday 20 August, and Chelsea is on it solo with Nathan in Queensland. She knows most of who will be there and the mingling is concentrated into morning tea, lunch and the end rather than the whole day. Heavy rain forecast for the day may well help the turnout — nobody will be in the orchard. Everything should be ready in time.
Anthony — Amos reckons Hamilton is the one most likely to get him to pick up the phone.

The Montague presentation Monday morning — 85–90% through and being cut back rather than added to. It covers why you would use one form over another, where acetates and sulfates fit and where they don’t, and it goes to the sales chat first for a factual once-over. Great Southern microbiome reports are landing, including an interesting fusarium one to go through with Grant.
Hussey’s Tuesday to knock over their soils, Brisbane Wednesday with Russell Barbrey and Elders, Bundaberg Thursday and back that night, office Friday.

Monday Zoom with Grant and a local grower on a metagenomic test. Catching up with Sam at DJ’s, who wants to do more work in strawberries. Program rounds, and a protected cropping day at Berri he is weighing up — a long way to go for one day.
Called out Amos against Challenge everything; no sacred cows. The point was not that every challenge changes the decision, but that people can raise one openly and know it will be heard.
A dense oat crop with a buggy in the stand. Bruce was away and the room did not know whether it was his own place or a client’s, so the location stays unlabelled until he confirms it.

Nate and Chelsea’s stand and story capture, together with the Apple Nutrition Playbook completed by Nate and Pia, were the other opening shots. The Cherry booklet had already generated strong inquiry and the smaller pile left over suggested the Apple booklet travelled well too, but Jamie still wants the direct grower feedback rather than reading too much into leftovers.

It may be a useful testing and advisory opportunity, but the contact, property details and yield figures heard in the recording are not confirmed.

August was tracking a little behind the revised profile. The budget had deliberately been pulled back slightly against last year and moved within Q1, with some work pushed into Q2, to reflect when the orders are expected to land. The gap was not read as lost business: a large volume was still sitting in quotes and the Fusion F order had gone through that morning.
Chelsea led month-to-date and financial-year-to-date; Hamilton was strong for the month; much of Nate’s expected volume was still in the quote pipeline. Margins were holding.
Soil tests were a little ahead of last year. Combined sap work was broadly level, but the mix had moved: AgVita SAP was ahead and NovaCrop DSA was behind.

The organic-related holds on the first overdue orders had effectively cleared. Most priority label approvals and heavy-metal results were back; two less-used labels were still to close out, and Paige will send the remaining heavy-metal samples. The expectation in the room was that the remainder should clear within about a week.

Two Handpicked Tasmania orders were due out that day and Montague Farms work was scheduled for the following week. Dry blends were about half a day behind and booked through Thursday 27 August. Liquids were three to four days behind, with catch-up planned early in the week of 24 August.
Will spend about half a day in the Wangaratta warehouse while in Victoria, both to help and to understand the manufacture, pick-pack and dispatch process properly.

Nathan narrowed the marketing read to reach, views, engagement and new followers. Not every platform is connected because some history sits behind paid integrations, but the four-week direction was up.

Fruit Growers Victoria gets a SWOT after Nathan returns. Great Southern Biology, Henty and early Christmas-hamper planning sit in the next month. Hamilton has been asked for a three-month view of small-crop opportunities; the same forward view is needed across the other segments so the marketing calendar can be built around what sales is actually approaching.

Inquiries have moved out of the Marketing tab into their own workflow, combining the useful Notion and Odoo history in one place. Paige enters new inquiries there and the team stops using Odoo Helpdesk for them. Website and manual inquiries feed the same list and trigger an SMS to Nathan and Jamie for fast follow-up.

Melbourne and Wangaratta Monday to Thursday for Josh Richardson’s start, office and target-list work, the Piangil discussion and time in the warehouse. Back in Perth Thursday and in the office Friday.
A reasonably open week to follow up the Queensland meetings and send the leaf- and soil-testing material back to the Bundaberg contacts.
Chase the testing for Jimmy, Piangil on Wednesday 26 August, and schedule the new-season leaf testing with Nate’s help. Use the open Monday and Friday slots to keep those moving.

Amos had the new product-by-product restriction sheet and would circulate it as the interim reference. Nathan’s follow-up was to bring the classifications into the dashboard price list so the sales team can see what a grower may use without translating the certificate each time.
Digesta remains the working product name. Grant had passed roughly a dozen launch-document questions to Isaac; the team launch information waits for those answers rather than filling the gaps itself.
No reply to the latest email. Hamilton will call.

Hamilton’s Queensland meetings with Neil and Russ Parberry surfaced a possible Elders pathway. Neil’s new-product role is looking for a dependable foliar calcium, a go-to plant stimulant and trace products that are easier to place commercially. Hamilton will prepare a product-and-placement list and keep exploring a working relationship with Russ.

Neil is considering more centralised soil-test intake, preferred laboratories and consistent output. The room could see a place for AI Ag in graphing and interpretation, but the support model matters: Elders would rather resell a supplier-supported range than carry the training burden of importing or owning a white label.

Existing Hybrid Ag products, a small distinct offer and some reformulation were all discussed. None was approved. The specialty-margin figures raised in the room were working numbers for the opportunity, not a new price decision.

The mixed-leaf crop is seeded together so it can be harvested as one mix. The photos showed substantial strike gaps. Seed depth was Hamilton’s first suspicion; blocked tubes, chemical effects and early laser-weeder scorch were also raised. None is a diagnosis yet because he had not worked through the failure with the grower.

The bed polisher followed ripping and bed forming as the third pass. Beds are remade for every crop, in places up to five times a year. The finish is excellent for seeding, but the repeated tillage remains the structural trade-off. The laser weeder footage showed the system in action without claiming a result.

Hamilton sampled potatoes from the area treated with Soil Primer and Nutrient Solubiliser. The canopy looked strong; there was no leaf result yet, so the photo is a sampling checkpoint rather than an efficacy claim.

The orchard was generally carrying good flower, with serious damage in local hotspots. The sequence showed spray burn, citrus blossom bug feeding and raceme dieback, with secondary fungal pressure discussed. Whether the insect vectors fungi or simply opens an infection point is unknown. Spraying had begun, but the meeting did not establish a treatment result.

Get the direct Fruit Growers Victoria feedback, follow up Nate on the tender raised in the sales segment, set Josh Richardson’s Monday-morning work and target list, and use the Victoria trip to build the warehouse understanding discussed in the meeting.

items.lead: The useful lesson and the gap
items.text: Jamie used it as an example of people synergy: someone returning with client history changed how the current result was understood. It also exposed a documentation weakness. Josh said the original reasoning was mainly in his head or an old email, so the long-term outcome could easily have lost its context.

Jamie spoke to roughly $1.45M month-to-date; the 11:40am Odoo pull used in the hero showed $1.48M. He wanted about $1.70M by this point against a $2.00M August budget. Most remaining quotes discussed with Nate were expected to land in September, so Jamie treated the balance as a real August shortfall and will build a recovery plan for next month.

Soil work was tracking well, while DSA/SAP volume was several hundred behind the usual year-to-date level. The room found several plausible contributors: horticulture had not reached its main testing window, broadacre crops were four to five weeks early, many recommendations reused last year’s SAP results, and Alex had contributed 81 August tests in the prior year. Jamie will drill into the split before treating it as missed opportunity.

The operations screen had stopped refreshing at 6pm on 27 August. That made several orders look overdue after their Odoo status had already moved. The meeting read must therefore be separated from the stale screen: most of the loads Amos walked through were delivered, dispatched or ready for collection.

A small vineyard order was still to go. Cherry Hill’s Flower-Cal work was expected early the following week, with no stocktake constraint identified; delivery by midweek was the working expectation rather than a confirmed dispatch.

The event campaign was running across social and email, with the nitrogen-use-efficiency webinar linked into the invitation. Click-through, registrations and attributable leads were not reported, so opens are the only campaign outcome established in this meeting.

SAP work on Monday, then Vic No-Till from 1–3 September. Bruce said a rebrand to Farmers Helping Farmers was expected, but the meeting did not confirm that change. Bruce’s Odoo calendar was not up to date when reviewed.

mtg-notes-0828.title: Technical huddle — method questions remain open

items.text: A garlic grower’s dry-ash results were showing unexpectedly high nitrate. The group discussed timing, nitrogen form and what each laboratory method is actually measuring, but did not reach a diagnosis.

NovaCrop DSA results appeared to show more sodium and chloride than the grower’s dry-ash results. After checking older olive SAPs, Josh said the sodium pattern looked similar across years and was probably not an issue. He also noted that dry ash expresses total elements against dry matter while sodium sits mainly in the soluble fraction, which can make the two methods read differently. Nate still planned to ask NovaCrop about the high-DSA versus low-to-mid dry-ash pattern.

The team weighed turnaround time against the value of a consistent long-term dataset. Switching laboratories case by case risks making trends harder to compare. AI Ag V3 and short interpretation masterclasses were floated as ways to make the accumulated data more useful; neither was approved as a project in this meeting.
Drill into the DSA/SAP gap, shape the September sales-recovery plan, finish mapping his own week with the team and get the Henty gazebo freighted from Albany.

gsbNotes.text: Four microbes selected as the highest organic-acid producers GSB could screen. They release phosphorus that is locked up — to calcium in high-pH soils, to iron and aluminium in low-pH — with gluconic acid doing most of the work and citric acid secondary. Only 20–30% of applied P is ever taken up; the rest fixes. Chemistry can break those bonds too, but it re-locks within a week, whereas the microbes keep doing it as long as they survive. Grant frames it as a soil conditioner, and was clear it is not the same job as Lockout.

The bigger idea underneath it, from Kamal: when phosphate is liberated, nitrogen availability rises with it — DNA synthesis needs phosphorus, and without it the plant can’t properly access nitrogen or the micronutrients either. That reframes SP from a phosphorus product into a nitrogen-efficiency product.

In the furrow. Liquid inject is the Rolls-Royce — and the reason matters: even where seed-applied fungicide kills a patch, you get re-inoculation once the fungicide dissipates. Seed coating loses on real estate rather than biology, because everything wants to be on the seed and there is usually a fungicide already there. A coated compost granule holds spores beautifully but costs the grower more. Ground spray is last and least targeted.

gsbNotes.lead: The only field result on SP
gsbNotes.text: A yield bump in canola on GSB’s local ground where phosphorus was locked up by aluminium. That is the whole evidence base Grant offered — unquantified, one site, one crop, no replication described, and nobody asked. Worth recording as exactly that.

Deliberately fungal-biased: three fungi plus an actinomycete, because in our farming systems the bacteria survive and the fungi don’t. Enzymatic breakdown of cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin and pectin — canola being the hard one on lignin. Take just 1% of the carbon out of that matter and the cementing holding the cell wall together fails, so it degrades fast. It colonises internally and works from the inside out, which Jimmy had seen in a trial near Albury.

gsbNotes.lead: And it competes for the substrate
gsbNotes.text: The same organisms consume the carbon and nitrogen that stubble-borne pathogens rely on, so there is less for them to carry into the next crop. GSB’s trial work used cereal stubble and compared treated against untreated and against a nutrition-only product. Grant’s competitive point: products that rely on enzymes or nutrition plus whatever biology is already in the paddock risk proliferating the resident pathogens along with everything else — his words were that they run a very real risk, not that it always happens.

Base recommendation is DigestMate onto stubble with about 8 kg/ha of ammonium sulfate. Be clear why: ammonium sulfate wins on economics, not biology. Urea works too and is slightly more complex for the microbes; amino acid and protein sources are fine; fish hydrolysate may be better again because the nitrogen is directly available. Nitrate is ruled out. Whether it is the ammonium or the sulfur doing the work was asked directly and never answered, so we can’t make a sulfur claim.

gsbNotes.lead: Rain, and how long it will wait
gsbNotes.text: It needs rain to be at its best but will sit on stubble from early summer after harvest and survive until it comes, within reason. Three months of 45°C will kill it. Apply any time after harvest.

It starts at the base of the stubble because that is where the residual moisture sits, so the field check is whether the stubble pulls out easily at the base. It will not look dramatic from the ute. The lab check is a C:N ratio before and after against an untreated control — a carbon reduction means it is working. Evidence to date is mostly South Australian cropping-belt grower feedback rather than replicated trials.

Three microbes on an endophytic Trichoderma backbone, all chosen as very rapid growers. They colonise the rhizosphere and phytosphere, out-populate anything pathogenic, steal its breakfast and then act as a bouncer on the door. Good results on high-Fusarium Queensland soils; currently being trialled in cotton on Verticillium. Grant was upfront: “by no means 100% effective 100% of the time — that’s not the world we live in in this biological space.”

gsbNotes.lead: Lockout is carbon-led, DigestMate is nitrogen-led
gsbNotes.text: Jamie asked whether Lockout’s food source follows the same principles. Grant started with “nitrogen, carbon” then corrected himself in the room and settled on more so carbon in that circumstance. A clean contrast between two products that otherwise sound like they want the same thing.

gsbNotes.lead: Lockout in orchards goes on at budswell
gsbNotes.text: Through budswell and certainly before flowering, to get colonisation established in the ground ahead of the pathogen becoming active. Grant, on the orchard he visited with Chelsea and Andrew where there is significant vascular disease. Lab reports are still pending, so his pathogen identification is a working assumption. This is the substance of the email he owes Chelsea.

gsbNotes.lead: Soil temperature — the fungi start at 5°C
gsbNotes.text: Bruce asked whether anything actually happens in the top 10 cm below 8°C. Kamal: the fungal side proliferates from 5°C, works across 5–30°C with an optimum around 25°C, but bacteria stall below about 15°C. Multiplication at 5–6°C is real, just slower. That is the honest answer to “it’s too cold for biology” on a winter-sown furrow — and a genuine point of difference against a bacterial-only inoculant. One to put back to GSB: the organism that differentiates SP is a bacterium, so cold-soil furrow work leans on the fungal fraction.

gsbNotes.lead: We are outnumbered about a thousand to one
gsbNotes.text: Kamal’s own arithmetic, and the most useful number in the meeting. We apply somewhere around 1–3 million cells; resident soil populations are around a billion per gram, and a heavy Fusarium load is a billion per gram on its own. That is why the food source isn’t optional, why proliferation rather than the applied dose does the work, and why a simple sugar feeds the wrong side. It also honestly qualifies the out-populate story above.

Grant flagged it unprompted: he does not use kill, suppress or control. The word is balance. Partly APVMA exposure, partly because it is the accurate description — nothing is being killed, it is being consumed, which leaves less opportunity for pathogens to proliferate. Worth adopting across our copy, and worth noting it rules out any claim framed as a reduction in disease incidence.

GSB has removed molasses as a food source entirely, and the same goes for glucose, sucrose and fructose. Simple sugars feed the resident pathogen load faster than they feed what we apply — see the thousand-to-one above. Use complex carbon instead: humic, fulvic, fish, seaweed. Kamal’s framing — molasses is fast food, humic is a meal you have to cook. One exception: where a test shows beneficials already outnumber pathogens, molasses is fine to push proliferation.

gsbNotes.lead: Nitrogen nutrition decides who you feed
gsbNotes.text: Jimmy put it up and Kamal confirmed it: feed a crop hard on nitrogen, accumulate nitrates, and the plant exudes free amino acids and simple sugars rather than complex ones — which is food for the pathogens rather than for the Trichoderma. It is the causal chain that connects a nutrition decision to a root-disease outcome without making a disease claim, and it explains why intensively fed horticulture gets root disease.

gsbNotes.lead: Carbon sets the recommendation, not soil type
gsbNotes.text: Asked which soil types suit, Kamal declined the texture framing entirely: it depends on carbon. Under 2% soil carbon, add a humic starter with the biology so it can fire up. Above 2%, he is not recommending humic or sugar at all. The best combination he named: a carbon source, a nitrogen source like fish, and a seaweed extract.

gsbNotes.lead: Carbon building is a five-to-ten-year play
gsbNotes.text: Fungal necromass is the stable form — melanin is very stable in soil. Kamal: visible at about five years, ten to judge it properly, and the fungal-to-bacterial rebalance sits on the same horizon. A strong year-one solubilisation response followed by tillage is a warning rather than a win, because year two it is gone. The room did not land on no-till dogma though: compacted ground needs oxygen for the fungi, and strategic tillage can sit alongside microbial application.

gsbNotes.lead: Liquid for foliar, powder for soil
gsbNotes.text: The liquid is roughly 80% metabolites and 20% spores. The metabolites do two jobs: inhibit pathogen growth, and signal the plant to switch on its own systemic resistance. That is why liquid beats powder as a foliar. Powder is mostly spores, which attach to carbon quickly and get through the rhizosphere — better for a root pathogen. And a granule and a powder are not the same thing.

A field rule that has nothing to do with GSB’s products and is immediately usable: never apply calcium when the stomata are shut — at night, or under scorching midday heat. Calcium moves on the transpiration stream, so apply when transpiration is running. The tell that it went on at the wrong time is calcium sitting in the leaf test while the fruit stays deficient, especially in citrus. This constrains our own standing Lockout mix, which carries PowerCal.

gsbNotes.lead: Calcium can re-fix what SP just released
gsbNotes.text: Kamal flagged the interaction: where you have plenty of phosphate-solubilising bacteria working, applied calcium can re-fix the phosphorus they just released, and pH wants to sit around seven. Whether he meant soil pH or tank pH wasn’t made clear — worth confirming before we put a number on it. Our standing cereal recipe pairs Lockout with humic and PowerCal, and the “is there anything else worth adding” question never got answered.

Never leave mixed product in a tank overnight. The spores go vegetative, block the sprayer, and die under pressure in that form. Spray pressure itself is not the problem — it is pressure over time, and a spray system only exposes them momentarily, so 15 bar in passing is fine. That is field experience rather than tested data. There is no EC or tank-concentration threshold — GSB has not trialled it and would not nominate a number.

Compatibility work exists for Trichoderma with a handful of registered fungicides and with glyphosate, but Grant framed that as a concession to grower nervousness rather than best practice — best practice is that the fungicide isn’t there and the pathogens are out-populated instead. His broader position on fungicide overuse driving resistant Fusarium, Verticillium and black root rot is strongly held; paraphrase it, don’t quote it. No compatibility statement was given for DigestMate with copper, despite the question naming copper.

Worth having straight for potato, cherry, avocado and tree-crop conversations. Phytophthora is an oomycete, not a true fungus, which is part of why fungicides have had a hard time with it — and it is picking up resistance to most of them. Its spores carry a flagellum and swim: a film of water, mist, fog or irrigation water and it moves through a block overnight. GSB’s answer is competition rather than control.

GSB’s metagenomic soil test reports carbon, the fungal-to-bacterial ratio, and counts of both pathogens and beneficials. Around 1 fungi to 50 bacteria is fine in high-nitrogen annuals like wheat, 1:20 is the aspiration, and worse than 1:100 is a problem. Horticulture wants fungal dominance — and GSB has never yet measured a fungal-dominant soil in their testing. It matters commercially: bacteria-dominant, the plant keeps only 20–30% of its photosynthate; balanced, it keeps 50–60%.

gsbNotes.lead: Compost teas — the objection is risk, not efficacy
gsbNotes.text: Grant conceded plainly that growers do get an effect and that increasing microbial diversity is a good thing they support. The objection is that on-farm brewing carries an unmanaged contamination risk, including a genuine health risk to anyone immunocompromised, and that the cost per microbe is poor against a manufactured product. If compost is used it needs to hit 70°C at the thermophilic stage and then humify — end up like a humic substance, not like compost — and every batch should be tested.

Kamal has run our FKF in the lab as a food source: Trichoderma proliferation was so high it filled a plate overnight, against the usual two days and two nights. He has already started recommending it to GSB’s own testers. One caveat — he suspects a preservative in it that suppresses the bacterial side; we need to confirm whether there is one. And a caution we raised ourselves: something that wins on a plate can still lose in the paddock if it is a simple sugar.

gsbNotes.lead: We still have no application rate
gsbNotes.text: The single biggest gap. Across the whole session the only rate given was the 8 kg/ha ammonium sulfate food source. Nothing on product rate, water rate, nozzle, filter, tank-mix order, jar test, seed-coat loading, granule blend rate, liquid or powder shelf life, or storage temperature. The granule figure of six months is borrowed off GSB’s rhizobium granules; they expect to beat it because these organisms are spore-formed, and Grant will review it in a few months. Registration status was never mentioned. First follow-up.

Grant is writing an agronomist’s summary covering all three products and where each best fits, and has already posted a paper on selecting microbial products by formulation type to the shared WhatsApp group — several of the team still need adding to it. We are to send food-source samples for plate testing, as single products and as mixtures, at recommended dose and at 1% and 2%. Andrew to supply the macadamia flower pathogen names and send diseased samples. Grant owes Chelsea the orchard email once the lab reports land. Next catch-up to be booked sooner than the last gap.

Whether DigestMate can be used in-crop, mid-season for disease protection was asked twice and drifted both times — no in-crop use is endorsed, and nobody should infer one. And horticultural leaf digestion has no trial data at all; Andrew is only just starting on nut trees, so any horticulture position is mechanism and theory only.
